newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Jockeying and mediation ahead of Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Jockeying and mediation ahead of Zaire talks.

text.p: Zaire's rebels talked tough on Monday, presenting this week's planned meeting between President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila as the veteran leader's last chance to quit with dignity.

South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who is trying to avert a bloody battle for Zaire's capital Kinshasa, said that Wednesday's meeting on board a South African naval ship could be the last hope for a peaceful settlement.

Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, seen by Mobutu supporters as the key to a political settlement of the seven-month-old civil war, returned to the capital Kinshasa to cheers from onlookers at its riverside port.
"The meeting on Wednesday may very well be the last chance to find a negotiated solution," Mbeki said in Cape Town.

Mobutu and Kabila met for the first time aboard the South African navy ice-breaker Outeniqua on May 4 and agreed to meet again to discuss arrangements for a transition to democracy. South Africa's President Nelson Mandela hosted the meeting.

Rebel spokesmen said in Lubumbashi on Monday that Mobutu was running out of time. "The meeting with Mobutu on Wednesday will be the second and last one and let no one make a mistake about that," rebel information chief Raphael Ngenda told Reuters.
"Our understanding is that we are going to the boat to accept Mobutu's resignation, nothing less, nothing more," Kabila's foreign affairs spokesman, Bizima Karaha, said.
"Wednesday will determine whether we make a soft landing in Kinshasa or a tough military entry."

Mbeki said that in the next 48 hours South African mediators would hold intensive discussions with Kabila, Mobutu, U.N. and Organisation of African Unity envoy Mohamed Sahnoun and various countries with an interest in ending the Zaire war.

Mbeki said he would probably travel to Zaire on Tuesday to hold separate meetings with Kabila and Mobutu. He identified the main issues as composition of a transitional authority, a timetable for setting it up and timing of Mobutu's resignation.
Mobutu supporters voted on Saturday to give Monsengwo back his old post as speaker of Zaire's transitional parliament, a job from which they helped oust him in 1995.
Monsengwo has yet to say whether he will take the job, which would make him the constitutional successor to Mobutu in the event of death or incapacity and a key player in a transition.
Mobutu, 66, suffers from cancer and has ruled Zaire since seizing power in 1965.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, control three quarters of Africa's third largest country.
Rebel commanders confirmed their forces had renounced a standstill pledge they gave to Mandela on May 4.
"We are advancing towards Kinshasa. Our forces are walking in all directions and our destination is the capital city," said Kabila's son Joseph, who is commander of rebel frontline units.
"The end should come very swiftly. I do not see the hold-out on Kinshasa lasting long. It will come in the next few days."
The rebels were last reported less than 200 km (125 miles) from the teeming capital of five million people.

They admit facing stiff resistance as they approach Kinshasa but say this is due to the presence of thousands of battle-hardened fighters from the Angola's rebel group UNITA -- whose supply line ran through Zaire.
The United States, meanwhile, cut the size of its Kinshasa embassy to 25 staff from 37. "It is one of a series of steps given the prevailing insecurity in Kinshasa," a diplomat said.
